title: Sequence to Sequence Learning
hook: Translate a sentence by reading it into one vector, then writing a new sentence out of that vector. This encoder–decoder recipe powered early neural machine translation.
key_points: An encoder RNN reads the input sequence and compresses it into a fixed-length vector.
A decoder RNN generates the output sequence from that vector, one token at a time.
Demonstrated strong results on English-to-French machine translation.
Reversing the input word order improved performance noticeably.
Established the encoder–decoder framework reused across many sequence tasks.
content_html: Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le showed you could map one sequence to another with a pair of recurrent networks: an encoder that reads the input and a decoder that writes the output. Applied to translation, this end-to-end neural approach reached results competitive with established systems and helped launch neural machine translation.
extra_html:
How it works

The encoder, an LSTM, reads the source sentence token by token and ends up with a single fixed-length vector meant to summarize the whole input. The decoder, another LSTM, takes that vector and generates the target sentence one word at a time, feeding each predicted word back in as context for the next. The authors found that reversing the order of the input words made the optimization easier and improved translation quality.

Why it matters

This paper crystallized the encoder–decoder pattern that underlies translation, summarization, and many other sequence-to-sequence tasks. Its main limitation — squeezing an entire sentence into one fixed vector — directly motivated the attention mechanism that followed, and ultimately the Transformer.

related.title: RNNs, LSTMs & Sequences
related.hook: To read a sequence, a network can loop over it one step at a time, carrying a memory of what came before. Plain RNNs forget fast; LSTMs add gates so they remember longer.

related.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
related.hook: Cramming a whole sentence into one vector loses information. This 2014 paper let the decoder look back at relevant source words at each step — the original attention mechanism.

flashcards.prompt: In the seq2seq model, what does the encoder produce from the input sentence?
flashcards.back_html: A single fixed-length vector meant to summarize the whole input, which the decoder then reads.

flashcards.prompt: What trick did the authors find improved translation quality?

choices.text: Reversing the order of the input words

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors found reversing the input word order made optimization easier and improved quality. Attention came later, in a different paper.

flashcards.prompt: What was the main limitation of the seq2seq encoder-decoder design?

choices.text: Squeezing the entire sentence into one fixed-length vector
It could not be trained end to end
It only worked on fixed-length inputs

flashcards.explanation_html: Forcing the whole input through one fixed vector was the bottleneck that directly motivated the attention mechanism.
